content: Professionals working in prosthetics and orthotics are encouraged to join and actively participate in professional associations and societies relevant to their field. This involvement helps to raise awareness about the profession and its importance. Both clinical and non-clinical professionals in this field are encouraged to establish their own professional associations or societies and connect them with regional and international federations and organizations. These professional bodies should support and promote evidence-based practices and develop a national ethical code of conduct. They can further advance the profession by sharing best practices through publications, networks, events, and refresher training for their members. Additionally, these organizations may engage with and advise regulators on codes of practice, participate in national planning, and promote their professional fields. Professional societies and associations can also be formed around specific topics, health conditions, or areas of knowledge to bring together interdisciplinary groups of personnel and stakeholders. These groups can share information about the treatment of specific conditions. Such organizations should allow membership for both professionals and users. Prosthetics and orthotics services should be user-centered, meaning they are planned from the perspective of the users and tailored to their needs, choices, and preferences in a humane and holistic manner. Service providers should have a written user policy in the local language that outlines how users and caregivers will be treated and how their rights will be upheld. All personnel should be adequately trained in this policy, and service providers should be able to demonstrate compliance with it. User-centered services should include features such as a user-friendly environment, respect for users, punctuality, safety, privacy, and confidentiality. Service units should be fully accessible, with clean, quiet, and comfortable waiting areas that provide adequate seating, pleasant temperatures, fresh air, and entertainment options for children. The relationship between providers and users should be built on dignity, empathy, mutual respect, honesty, and trust. Personnel should maintain a professional and polite attitude, communicate effectively, and listen attentively to users. They should also respect local cultural norms in their attire. Services should be delivered promptly, without unnecessary delays, and scheduled appointment times should be respected. Safety measures must be in place to protect users from injury, health hazards, and any form of verbal or physical abuse. Privacy should be ensured during all phases of treatment, and personal information should be treated as confidential. Users should be asked for consent before their images or videos are used in any context. Service users and caregivers should receive complete information about the treatment process, proposed interventions, expected outcomes, and potential risks. They should also be informed about follow-up care, maintenance of prosthetic or orthotic devices, and where to access repair services. This information should be accessible, such as being printed in large formats and local languages. Users should have the final say in their treatment decisions and should be supported in making informed choices. They should be free to choose from available alternatives, including components, materials, and designs, and their participation should always be voluntary. Users and caregivers should also have full access to their clinical records to actively participate in their treatment and decision-making. Service providers should establish systems for users and caregivers to provide feedback, including opportunities for anonymous complaints and suggestions. Special attention should be given to protecting vulnerable individuals, such as women and children. Users should have the right to request treatment from personnel of the same gender and to be accompanied if they wish. Service users should not be regarded merely as recipients of care but as partners who can contribute to improving and sustaining services. They and their families possess critical knowledge that ensures services are of high quality and adapted to their needs. Users should be involved in planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating services at all levels through their representatives, such as user groups and organizations for disabled individuals. These representatives should participate in relevant decision-making committees and advisory boards. Users have the right to choose their service provider and prosthetic or orthotic technology. This right promotes healthy competition, which can improve the quality and cost-effectiveness of services. Users should be informed about their options, including providers with the appropriate expertise, how to access services, and whether fees apply or are covered by insurance or welfare schemes. They should also have the opportunity to choose the type of components, materials, and design of their prosthesis or orthosis, within the limits of available financing or reimbursement. Service providers and national stakeholders must ensure equal access to services for all individuals in need, regardless of disability, health condition, or socioeconomic status. Services must be financially, physically, geographically, socially, linguistically, and organizationally accessible. Financially, services should be affordable for all, including poor and vulnerable populations. Physically, service units should be designed to accommodate individuals with restricted mobility, with features such as ramps, lifts, and accessible parking. Geographically, services should be available to all users, requiring a network of service units distributed throughout the country or decentralization of services. Socially, services should be offered equitably to all individuals, regardless of gender, age, social background, ethnicity, cultural values, religion, beliefs, sexual orientation, or refugee status. Linguistically, users should be able to communicate with providers in their own language, and information materials should be available in local languages and accessible formats. Organizationally, opening hours, waiting times, and appointment systems should accommodate all users, including those from remote locations or those who work during the day. Prosthetics and orthotics services can be provided by public, private (for-profit or not-for-profit), and non-governmental or philanthropic organizations. Most countries will require a combination of different service providers to ensure equitable access to affordable, high-quality services for all. Public service providers, such as government-run units, must ensure that services are available at an affordable cost for everyone. Private for-profit providers can stimulate competition, potentially reducing costs and increasing quality, but they often require subsidies or insurance coverage to remain viable. Private not-for-profit entities, such as social enterprises, reinvest profits into services for the benefit of poor users. Non-governmental and philanthropic organizations may also play a role in providing services in some countries.
